title: Listening counts too
hook: the tradition forbids listening to gossip, not only speaking it

segments.voice: Yesterday: feathers in the wind. Your line was you can't gather feathers. Before which sentence did you pause? Today closes a week about speech by turning to the other side of every conversation. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-four.

Gossip is a two-person job. One to say it, and one to lean in. Watch a conversation where someone lowers their voice and says, "Okay, don't repeat this." The listener's face does half the work: eyebrows up, chair pulled closer, "No. Tell me everything." Without that face, gossip can die in the first sentence. All week the focus has been on the mouth. Jewish teaching on speech doesn't let the ear off the hook as an innocent bystander. Today is about the listener.
screen: `GOSSIP NEEDS TWO.` → `THE LISTENER LEANS IN.` → `THE EAR IS NOT A BYSTANDER.`

segments.voice: Listening counts too. Turn it four ways. First, the verse. In Exodus, among the laws for honest courts: "Thou shalt not utter a false report." The rabbis of the Talmud read that line in two directions at once: don't spread a false report, and don't take one in. The same verse that guards the mouth guards the ear. Second, the body. The Talmud, in tractate Ketubot, asks a playful question: why are human fingers shaped like pegs? So that if a person hears something unfit, they can put their fingers in their ears. And why is the ear hard, but the earlobe soft? So the lobe can be folded in to close it. It's half a smile and half serious: the body comes with a way to stop listening built in. The ear can close. Most of the time nobody needs to plug it. Knowing it can close is the point. Third, what not listening looks like. It's rarely a speech. Changing the subject. Asking, "Should we be talking about this?" Finding a reason to refill the coffee. And if the words have already landed, the teachers of speech, the Chafetz Chaim among them, ask the listener at least not to believe it, to hold it as unproven rather than true. Fourth, the week behind us. It began with responsibility, carrying your share. Then lashon hara, harmful truth. The Chafetz Chaim and his book on guarding the tongue. Rechilut, carrying tales. Motzi shem ra, a false bad name. Feathers that can't be gathered. And now the ear. Each piece closes a door, and this one closes the last door: gossip with nobody to hear it has nowhere to go.
screen: `DON'T SPREAD IT, DON'T TAKE IT IN.` · `FINGERS SHAPED LIKE PEGS.` · `CHANGE THE SUBJECT, OR DOUBT IT.` · `A WEEK OF GUARDED SPEECH.` · then, large: `DON'T LISTEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk away from gossip. You'll rehearse it here, so it's ready when you need it. Settle, and breathe. Picture a place where talk about other people tends to start: a break room, a family dinner, a group chat that lights up at night. See the moment it begins, the lowered voice, the "did you hear." Now choose your exit. Maybe a question: "Is this ours to talk about?" Maybe a new topic. Maybe just standing up to get water. Play it through once, calmly, until it feels like something you could actually do. If you pray, you can ask in your own words for ears that know when to close. The bell holds the time.
Listening counts too. In Jewish teaching on speech, hearing gossip and accepting it is part of the harm, not just saying it. Today's word.

Your line: don't listen. Today, when talk about someone who isn't there begins, take the exit you rehearsed, and if you've already heard it, hold it as unproven. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-four.

howItsDone: Jewish laws of speech, as the Chafetz Chaim sets them out, treat listening to and believing lashon hara as forbidden alongside speaking it; observant Jews try to change the subject or leave when gossip starts.

fork.setup: a friend leans in: "okay, don't repeat this, but..." about someone you both know. what do you do?
options: lean in; you won't repeat it, so it's harmless.
steer the talk elsewhere, or step away.
listen, then tell the person it's about.
fork.reveal: Jewish teaching on speech counts the listener too: hearing and accepting it is part of the harm, and carrying it on would be rechilut.

trapdoor: what you thought: gossip is the talker's problem.
what it means: the listener is part of it, and can end it by not taking it in.
what a scholar hears: the Talmud reads Exodus 23:1 as forbidding both spreading and accepting a false report, and Ketubot pictures fingers and earlobes made for closing the ear.
recall: the same roles for women and men

notes: Exodus 23:1 quoted from JPS 1917; confirm wording.
The reading of 'lo tisa' as also 'do not accept' a false report is attributed to the Talmud (Pesachim 118a; also Makkot 23a). Confirm the citation.
Ketubot 5b (Bar Kappara on fingers shaped like pegs; the school of Rabbi Yishmael on the soft earlobe) paraphrased; confirm. Arakhin 15b ('kills three') was avoided because day 1269 uses it.
Chafetz Chaim's rule that one who hears lashon hara should not believe it (may take precaution but not accept it as true) is paraphrased; confirm.
